::: {#rem-expectation-generalizes-population-mean}
#### The expectation extends the population mean to populations without a finite size

Group the units of a finite population by their values,
as in the proof of @prp-population-mean-expectation:
$n_y$ of the $n$ units have value $y$.
Then the population mean is

$$
\avgin a_i = \sum_{y} y \cd \frac{n_y}{n},
$$

a sum over the distinct values, each weighted by its relative frequency $n_y / n$.
For a unit [chosen at random](probability-basics.qmd#def-random-choice),
that relative frequency is the [probability mass function](random-variables.qmd#def-pmf) of its value:
$\P(Y = y) = n_y / n$.

The [definition of expectation](#def-expectation) keeps the formula
and replaces the relative frequencies with probabilities:
$\E{X} = \sum_{x} x \cd \P(X = x)$.
That version no longer needs a population size $n$ to divide by,
so it also covers random variables that no finite population produces:

- a [discrete random variable](random-variables.qmd#def-discrete-rv) with infinitely many possible values,
  such as the number of trials before the first success,
  where the sum has infinitely many terms;
- a [continuous random variable](random-variables.qmd#def-continuous-rv),
  where every single value has probability $0$,
  so the [density](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) takes the place of the relative frequencies
  and an integral takes the place of the sum:
  $\E{X} = \int x \cd \p(X = x)\,dx$.

So the expectation is the population mean of a population that may be infinite,
described by its distribution rather than by a list of its units.

:::
